# Decoding the Old Honda 2+3 Pin DLC: Why ISO 9141 Fails on US Models

Working with legacy vehicle diagnostics often feels like debugging hardware you can't touch. A common stumbling block involves early 2000s Hondas equipped with the older 2+3 pin Data Link Connector (DLC). Unlike modern vehicles that strictly adhere to SAE J1962 OBD-II standards, these pre-2001 models often use a proprietary ISO 9141-2 K-Line protocol. The confusion usually stems from mixing up regional specifications and misunderstanding how legacy pins map to the physical connector used in later years.

### The Pinout vs. Reality Gap

For vehicles built between 1996 and 2000, specifically US-market Civics like the D16Y8 model found in a 2000 iSR, the situation is tricky. While the external 3-pin DLC (two power pins and one signal pin) technically follows ISO 9141-2, the wiring inside the vehicle often diverges from international standards.

The standard ISO 9141 pinout for a 3-pin connector defines Pin 7 as the K-Line (signal), with B+ and Ground on the other pins. If you connect an ElmScan5 or similar hardware to these three wires, expecting the tool to recognize the protocol immediately, you will likely fail. Tools like ScanTool.net or generic OBD-II scanners often assume a standard J1962 layout where Pin 7 is K-Line, but they may not correctly interpret the specific handshake sequences or baud rates (typically 5 baud initialization followed by 10.4 kbps) required for ISO 9141-2 on Honda ECUs of this era.

### The US WSM Anomaly

The root cause of communication failures often lies in how General Motors and Honda handled the transition to OBD-II in North America. In the United States, manufacturers were mandated to use the standard 16-pin DLC connector by 1996. Consequently, many vehicles that still utilized older ECUs or internal wiring schemes ended up with a hybrid setup: an external 3-pin connector for legacy accessories or specific diagnostics, but an internal PCM (Powertrain Control Module) wired according to the US OBD-II standard.

When examining service manuals like the WSM for US Civics (1996–2000), you will find that Pin 7 on the external DLC is frequently unconnected in these specific models. Instead, the K-Line signal is routed through a different path within the vehicle's harness, often appearing at Pin 15 of the internal 16-pin connector or via a dedicated wire (such as the blue/yellow wire labeled "K-Line" on the PCM side). This creates a scenario where the external ISO 9141 pinout is physically present but electrically isolated from the ECU's communication loop.

### Protocol Matching and Tool Limitations

This discrepancy explains why standard diagnostic software fails. Tools designed for universal OBD-II compliance expect strict adherence to J1962 pin mappings. When they probe Pin 7 on a US-model Honda with a 3-pin adapter, they find nothing or incorrect voltage levels because the signal is bypassed entirely in favor of the internal architecture.

To successfully read ECU data from these vehicles using tools like an ElmScan5, you must treat the connection as a custom hardware interface rather than a plug-and-play OBD session. You cannot rely on the software to auto-detect the protocol if the physical layer doesn't match expectations. The solution often involves bypassing the external 3-pin connector entirely and accessing the K-Line directly at the PCM or using a specialized adapter that bridges the internal pins correctly.

In cases where you must stick with the external 3-pin DLC, you are essentially working against a non-standard implementation of ISO 9141-2. The vehicle is technically OBD-II compliant in terms of mandate but uses legacy communication hardware internally. This requires a deeper understanding of the specific model year's wiring diagram to map the correct pins to your scanner, rather than relying on generic pinout tables found online for "Honda OBD1" or early "OBD2A/B" classifications.
